blocks.text: That is, if we conjecture rightly, the Greek translators read the Hebrew words יצוא ושוב, going out and returning, as ולוא ישוב, and it did not return. Literally [col. 212] and it will not return. But the future for the past occurs so frequently that in Psalm 107 alone one can find at least twenty examples of this κατάχρησις [katachrēsis]. Nor do יצוא ושוב and ולוא ישוב differ much in writing. For in old manuscripts the letters Vau and Iod are so similar that they are very often interchanged. And Lamed differs from Tsade almost only by its horn: Tsade has it on the right and lower, Lamed on the left and higher. Those who are accustomed to reading the Rabbis know what I mean. Here, then, if I am not mistaken, is the true origin of the different reading and rendering of these words. Nor would I readily say which is to be preferred. And although I am accustomed to revere the Hebrew reading, so that I never depart from it except very reluctantly, I nevertheless admit that in this passage the Greek is clearer: The raven went out, and did not return until etc., that is, it never returned to the ark. But, they say, if it did not return, what became of it? Augustine answers in his sixth Tractate on John: It died in these waters. And [II, 804] in Against Faustus, book 12, chapter 20: The raven, when sent out, did not return, being either overtaken by the waters or lured by some floating corpse. And Cyril in the Glaphyra, book 2: Ἐνεπνίγη δὲ, οἶμαι, τοῖς ὕδασιν, ἔρεισμά τε, καὶ στάσιν οὐχ εὑρηκώς· [Enepnigē de, oimai, tois hydasin, ereisma te, kai stasin ouch heurēkōs] It was drowned, I think, in the waters, since it had not found where to stand. This can be granted without risk. And it is objected in vain that the species of ravens could not have been restored after the flood from a single surviving raven. For that raven could have mated with the female before it was sent out. Indeed, there are some among the Hebrews who hold that it was sent out by Noah for precisely this reason, that it had polluted and defiled the ark with untimely lust. The raven could also have survived even though it did not return to the ark, whether by perching on a corpse floating on the waters, or on the mountain tops, which had already begun to be laid bare of the waters forty days before it was sent out, Gen. VIII, 5. 6. 7. Why then was the dove, sent out seven days later, forced to return to the ark, not finding where to set its foot, because the waters still lay over the whole earth, Gen. VIII, 8? I answer: First, it is asserted without grounds that the dove was sent out seven days after the raven. Noah did indeed send it out ὀπίσω αὐτοῦ [opisō autou] after it, that is, after the raven, if we follow the Greeks and Jerome; but Moses does not even say this. His words are: And he sent out the dove מאתו from himself, as Jonathan, Onkelos, the Syriac, the Samaritan and both Arabic versions rightly render it. So the raven and the dove could have been sent out at the same time. But suppose the dove was sent out after the raven: what need was there to delay this sending for seven days, when, the raven not having returned, Noah could have sent it out on the very next day? Second, the dove returned because it does not willingly set its foot in wet and marshy places. But the raven, being of a very dry temperament, is known to delight greatly in water. Hence ravens, sensing coming rain, give many signs of joy, both by their voice and by the movement of their wings, as can be seen in Aratus, line 963 etc. Because φιληδοῦσι τοῖς ὑγροῖς [philēdousi tois hygrois], they delight in moist things, as Theon puts it there.
The pagan fable of the raven also seems to favour the Greek reading: sent by Apollo to fetch water, it did not return until the figs were ripe. Ovid, Fasti, book 2:
Forgetful of its orders, it is said to have sat beneath a tree, Until the fruit grew sweet with slow delay.
